lead: Fault-tolerant quantum computation runs gates and measurements on encoded qubits so that one physical fault cannot become a logical error. Quantum error correction stores a logical qubit safely, but a gate can spread one error to many qubits. Fault tolerance adds careful circuit design, fresh ancillas and verified syndrome extraction. It is the bridge from small noisy machines to long algorithms such as Shor's factoring, and to any future quantum computer that must run for hours without restarting.
prereq: You need: 5.7 quantum error-correcting codes and Unit 3 universal gates (CNOT, Hadamard, T gate).

sections.h3: Why a code is not enough

blocks.text: A quantum error-correcting code protects a resting logical qubit. It does not protect a computation by itself. A physical gate touches one or two qubits, but a logical gate uses many physical gates. If one physical gate fails, the fault can move through later gates and become errors on several qubits in the same code block. Two such errors can defeat a code built to correct one error.

Fault-tolerant computation designs every operation so that one physical fault creates at most one error in each logical block. The error stays correctable. This is stricter than adding a code: it constrains gates, measurements, state preparation and idle times. A useful rule is to check every place where a single control qubit touches many targets; a bad control spreads its error to every target.

A transversal gate acts on one or two code blocks. For a single-qubit gate it applies the same physical gate to every qubit of a block. For a two-qubit gate it applies physical gates between corresponding qubits of two blocks, touching each physical qubit at most once. A transversal CNOT between two logical qubits is a set of physical CNOTs: physical qubit i of the control block to physical qubit i of the target block. If one physical CNOT fails, only one pair is affected; the error does not hop between pairs. For the seven-qubit Steane code, transversal CNOT, Hadamard and phase gates are all available. The nine-qubit Shor code gives a transversal CNOT but not a transversal Hadamard. CNOT, Hadamard and phase gates together generate the Clifford group. The transversal gates of a code form a subgroup of the Clifford group; for the Steane code this subgroup includes CNOT, Hadamard and phase.

Clifford gates alone are not universal. A non-Clifford gate, such as the T gate or Toffoli, needs a special encoded state. The state is prepared repeatedly and purified by magic-state distillation; the name is enough here. The distilled state is consumed to apply the gate fault-tolerantly. Some syllabi call this whole subject 'fault-tolerant quantum computation'.

A syndrome extraction circuit couples data qubits to an ancilla prepared in |0> for Z-type stabilizers and in |+> for X-type stabilizers. The ancilla is measured; the data are not measured. For fault tolerance the ancilla should be fresh or verified. This makes an ancilla fault unlikely to pass into the data, but does not rule it out: an undetected ancilla error can still enter the data. One method uses several ancillas to prepare a verified cat state, then couples it to the data. The measurement outcome is a syndrome bit. Repeating extraction and checking consistency prevents a single ancilla fault from being read as a data error.

blocks.where: p_L is logical error per gate; p is physical error per operation; p0 is a constant from the code and circuit; p_th is the threshold; k is the number of concatenation levels.

blocks.text: Concatenation puts a logical qubit inside another code. If one level reduces the logical error rate from p to c p², then k levels give roughly the formula above. The threshold theorem states that if p is below a constant p_th, concatenation makes p_L arbitrarily small with overhead that grows only polylogarithmically in the computation length. Typical threshold estimates are around 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁴ for concatenated codes under realistic noise models, with optimistic ideal-circuit estimates near 10⁻³. Surface codes reach about 10⁻², which is why hardware groups favour them. Detailed threshold calculations are beyond this unit.

examples.question: A logical gate is built from three physical gates. Each physical gate fails independently with probability p = 0.001. The logical gate fails only if two or more of the three physical gates fail. Find the logical failure probability. Give the exact value and the value rounded to one significant figure.
steps: The failure event is: exactly two gates fail, or all three gates fail.
Number of ways to choose exactly two failing gates: C(3,2) = 3.
Probability that a chosen pair fails and the third works: p²(1−p) = (0.001)² × 0.999 = 9.99 × 10⁻⁷.
examples.answer: The exact logical failure probability is 2.998 × 10⁻⁶, about 3 × 10⁻⁶.
examples.check:
p = 0.001
p_two = 3 * p**2 * (1 - p)
p_three = p**3
p_fail = p_two + p_three
print(p_fail)
print(float(f'{p_fail:.0e}'))

traps: Fault tolerance is not the same as quantum error correction. A code protects stored qubits; fault tolerance also protects gates, measurements and ancilla preparation.
A single fault must not spread to two errors in one block. A control qubit touching many targets is a common spread path.
The threshold theorem needs p below p_th. Adding more code levels when p is above threshold makes logical errors worse.
Transversal Clifford gates are not universal. A non-Clifford gate needs magic-state distillation, not just more CNOTs.
Ancilla measurement gives the syndrome; measuring data qubits destroys the encoded state.

quiz.q: Define a transversal gate in one sentence.
quiz.a: A transversal gate acts on one or two code blocks: it applies the same physical gate to every qubit of a block (single-qubit gate) or between corresponding qubits of two blocks (two-qubit gate), touching each physical qubit at most once.

quiz.q: Why can a single physical fault become a logical error if a logical gate uses many physical gates?
quiz.a: The fault can propagate through later gates and affect several qubits. If two errors land in one block, a one-error-correcting code fails.

quiz.q: A logical gate has four physical gates, each failing with p = 0.01. It fails if two or more fail. Compute the logical failure probability.
A student says 'We use the nine-qubit code, so every gate is automatically fault-tolerant.' What is wrong?
quiz.a: The code only protects storage. Logical gates and syndrome extraction need designs that stop one fault from spreading to two errors, and the physical error rate must be below threshold.

quiz.q: What is the role of a fresh ancilla in syndrome extraction?
quiz.a: It interacts with the data qubits and is then measured, giving syndrome information without measuring the data. Using a fresh or verified ancilla makes it unlikely that an ancilla fault passes into the data, but does not make it impossible.

quiz.q: State the threshold theorem in one sentence.
quiz.a: If the physical error rate is below a constant threshold, concatenated fault-tolerant codes can make the logical error rate arbitrarily small with overhead polylogarithmic in computation length.

quiz.q: Why is concatenation not useful when p = 0.1 and p_th = 0.01?
quiz.a: Because p is above p_th, each encoding level increases the logical error rate; more levels make it worse.

quiz.q: A code reduces error from p to c p² with c = 100. For p = 10⁻³, what is the one-level logical error per gate? Is it below p?

beyond: Not for the exam. Real hardware groups study surface codes and lattice surgery because they tolerate higher physical error rates than concatenated codes. Magic-state distillation is a major cost in resource estimates for Shor's algorithm. Cloud quantum processors now expose error-mitigation tools, not full fault tolerance. Search next for 'surface code threshold', 'lattice surgery' and 'magic state distillation'.
